name: Executive order of May 22, 1856 setting apart the Mendocino Indian reservation, California
citation: Executive order of May 22, 1856, under the Act of March 3, 1853
nations: Pomo peoples of the Mendocino coast
promises: Under the Act of March 3, 1853, which authorized military reserves for Indian purposes in California of not more than 25,000 acres each, President Pierce set apart the Mendocino reserve on the recommendation of Superintendent Henley (Royce).

Royce describes the tract as running along the coast from the south bank of the Noyo River to a point one mile north of the mouth of Hale (Bee-da-loe) Creek, and inland to include the valleys beyond the first range of hills.
compensation: None to the Indians was found. The 1868 Act directed that the land be surveyed and sold at not less than $1.25 an acre, that buyers pay for United States improvements, and that persons who had made improvements on the reservation keep them with first right to buy 640 acres.
today: Royce gives the reserve's actual abandonment for Indian purposes as March 31, 1866. Congress restored the reservation to the public lands by section 6 of the Act of July 27, 1868 (ch. 248, sec. 6, 15 Stat. 198, 223), with no provision for the Indians who had lived on it. That Act is the separate entry cession-1868-07-27-mendocino-indian-reservation.

sources.title: Charles C. Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (18th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899), schedule pp. 816-817
Act of July 27, 1868, ch. 248, sec. 6, 15 Stat. 198, 223 (Mendocino Indian reservation restored to the public lands)

openQuestions: This record is the reserve's establishment; the 1868 restoration is a separate queue entry (cession-1868-07-27-mendocino-indian-reservation, same Royce area 522). Under Jordan's rule the end of a reservation set apart by executive order is not by itself a breach, and the 1868 Act is treated the same way here, as for the Round Valley Act of 1873, until a court, claims-commission or government finding about it is found.

Searched for findings: ICC full text for Mendocino with 1856 and Noyo (no hits), the 1885 Dawes report on California reservations (mentions Mendocino County only), and the Court of Claims Indians of California opinion of 1942 (98 Ct. Cl. 583, no mention). See the audit line below on the 1944 offset judgment.
Royce's note gives the Commissioner's recommendation as August 16, 1856 and the order as May 22, 1856; one of the two dates is likely misprinted in the scan.
No Pomo tribal account of the Mendocino reservation was found; secondary accounts of removals to Round Valley turned up in search but were not opened.
treaties.json lists no present-day tribes; which Pomo nations descend from the reservation's people (Sherwood Valley, Coyote Valley, Pinoleville and others, and Round Valley) was not settled.

Audit 2026-11-08: citation corrected from 15 Stat. 221, 223 to 15 Stat. 198, 223: chapter 248 (the Indian appropriation act of July 27, 1868) begins at p. 198 (govinfo); sec. 6 at p. 223 was read and matches the compensation line.

Audit 2026-11-08: the 1944 Court of Claims offset judgment (Indians of California, 102 Ct. Cl. 837, December 4, 1944) is not in the Caselaw Access Project and no free copy was found, so whether Mendocino land was among the 611,226 acres of reservation land charged as an offset could not be checked. The 1964 ICC compromise findings (13 Ind. Cl. Comm. 369) mention the offset only in total; the 1935, 1942 and 1943 Court of Claims opinions do not mention Mendocino. Senate Report No. 1522 (1885, Dawes) was searched: it names the Mendocino reservation only as the reserve to which Nome Cult was auxiliary in 1856, with no finding about its end. Royce p. 851 checked: Henley recommendation of Nov. 17, 1855 and order of May 22, 1856 confirmed. No change to status.
